0.name: Balgarski natsionalen front
0.text:
The Bulgarian National Front was founded in Munich in 1947 by exiles, most of them veterans of the Union of Bulgarian National Legions, who had fled the communist takeover. Its chairman Ivan Dochev, the former Legions leader, directs it from Canada, and it keeps branches in the United States, Western Europe and South America around its journal Svoboda.

The Front seeks the overthrow of communism and a strong, authoritarian national state allied with the United States and NATO, and it cherishes the dream of a Bulgaria united with Macedonia. It is active in the World Anti-Communist League and lobbies conservative circles in Washington and Ottawa. Its leverage lies in émigré networks, Western anti-communist patrons and broadcasts aimed at Bulgarians at home.

1.name: Balgarski zemedelski naroden sayuz – Nikola Petkov
1.english: Bulgarian Agrarian National Union – Nikola Petkov
1.native_full: Balgarski zemedelski naroden sayuz – Nikola Petkov
1.text:
The Bulgarian Agrarian National Union – Nikola Petkov is the independent agrarian movement that refused to serve the communists after 1944. Petkov, who led the opposition to nearly a third of the vote in the rigged elections of October 1946, was hanged in September 1947 despite Western protests, and his party was dissolved. In exile it is led from Washington by Georgi Mihov Dimitrov, known as Gemeto, who also heads the Bulgarian National Committee, while its veterans at home keep silent.

It stands for Aleksandar Stamboliyski's agrarian democracy: a nation of free peasant proprietors, voluntary cooperatives, parliamentary government, civil liberties and friendship with the Western democracies. Its leverage lies in the memory of Petkov's martyrdom among the peasantry, the legitimacy of the 1946 vote and its Western émigré networks.

2.name: Lyutite chushki
2.text:
The Hot Peppers take their name from Radoy Ralin's book of satirical epigrams Lyuti chushki, published in 1968 with drawings by Boris Dimovski and pulped when censors decided that a pig's curly tail resembled Todor Zhivkov's signature. The scandal made Ralin the symbol of a liberal intelligentsia that includes writers such as Blaga Dimitrova and Valeri Petrov, the philosopher Zhelyu Zhelev, expelled from the party in 1965, and the playwright Georgi Markov, who defected to the West in 1969.

They want freedom of expression, an end to censorship, the rule of law and a socialism that tolerates criticism and contact with the West. They have no organisation, only friendships, cafés and whispered jokes. Their leverage lies in their wit, their popularity and the fear their ridicule inspires in the powerful.

3.name: Balgarska rabotnicheska sotsialdemokraticheska partiya
3.text:
The Bulgarian Social Democratic Workers' Party, the 'Broad Socialists' who parted from the Narrow Socialists in 1903, was crushed between 1946 and 1948. Its independent wing under Kosta Lulchev and Krastyu Pastuhov went into opposition; Pastuhov died in prison in 1949 and Lulchev spent years behind bars, while the fusionist wing merged into the Communist Party. Veterans such as Petar Dertliev, survivors of the camps, keep its ideas alive in private, and its exiles maintain ties with the Socialist International.

It stands for parliamentary democracy, free trade unions, a mixed economy and social welfare on the Scandinavian model. Its old base of railwaymen, teachers and skilled workers has aged, and its leverage lies in its exile contacts with Western labour parties and a reputation for integrity.
3.wiki: Bulgarian Social Democratic Workers' Party (Broad Socialists)

4.name: Balgarska komunisticheska partiya
4.text:
The Bulgarian Communist Party, heir of the Narrow Socialists of 1903 and of Georgi Dimitrov, has ruled Bulgaria since the coup of 9 September 1944. Todor Zhivkov has been First Secretary since 1954 and Chairman of the Council of Ministers since 1962; the plot of 1965 against him was crushed. Georgi Traykov of the allied Agrarian Union serves as head of state.

The party is Moscow's most loyal ally, so close that Zhivkov has proposed merging Bulgaria into the Soviet Union, and its troops entered Czechoslovakia in 1968. At home it has collectivised agriculture, built heavy industry on Soviet credit and opened the Black Sea coast to Western tourists. Its leverage is total: the nomenklatura, the Fatherland Front, State Security and the army.

5.name: Federatsiya na anarhokomunistite v Balgariya
5.english: Federation of Anarchist Communists of Bulgaria
5.text:
The Federation of Anarchist Communists of Bulgaria, founded in 1919, was once among the strongest anarchist movements in Europe, rooted among peasants, teachers and workers. The communists suppressed it after 1944 and sent hundreds of its members to the camps of Belene and elsewhere; survivors live under surveillance at home, while exiles such as Georgi Grigoriev, who writes as G. Balkanski in Paris, keep its press alive.

It rejects the state, the party dictatorship and capitalism alike, calling for free communes, self-management by workers and peasants, and federation from below. The anarchists denounce Zhivkov's regime as state capitalism and greet the student revolts of 1968 in the West as proof that their ideas live. Their leverage is tiny but stubborn: veterans' networks and illegal leaflets.
5.wiki: Federation of Anarchist Communists of Bulgaria

6.name: Chervenkovistite
6.text:
The Chervenkovists are the Stalinist veterans who served Valko Chervenkov, Georgi Dimitrov's brother-in-law and Bulgaria's 'little Stalin' from 1950 to 1956. Chervenkov was demoted after the April Plenum of 1956, dropped from the Politburo in 1961 and expelled from the party in 1962, but in 1969, as Soviet power crushed the Prague Spring, Zhivkov had his membership restored, a gesture the old guard read as vindication.

They want rigid central planning, militant atheism, ideological purity in culture and an end to the creeping consumerism of the Black Sea resorts, with their Western tourists, jeans and rock music. Unconditionally loyal to Moscow, they see every reform as a step toward Czechoslovak heresy. Their leverage lies in the party apparatus, the security services and Soviet trust in uncompromising comrades.

7.name: Darzhavna sigurnost
7.text:
State Security is Bulgaria's political police, organised within the Ministry of Internal Affairs under Minister Angel Solakov and modelled closely on the Soviet KGB, with which it works hand in glove. It runs counter-intelligence, foreign espionage and the struggle against 'ideological diversion', and it administered the labour camps of Belene and Lovech until they were closed in the early 1960s.

As a power bloc it stands for order, vigilance and loyalty to Moscow. It watches the intelligentsia, the churches, the Turkish and Pomak minorities, the émigrés and every Western tourist, and through firms such as Kintex it shares in foreign trade and smuggling. Its leverage lies in its files, its informers, its hard-currency operations and its direct line to the KGB.

8.name: Demir Baba Erenleri
8.text:
The Devotees of Demir Baba are the Alevi, or Kızılbaş, communities of north-eastern Bulgaria, tens of thousands of Turkish-speaking villagers in the Deliorman around Razgrad and Shumen, with kin in the Kardzhali region. Their spiritual centre is the sixteenth-century tekke of Demir Baba near Sveshtari, a domed shrine where pilgrims still gather, guided by hereditary dedes who keep the rites of the Babai and Bektashi traditions.

They revere Ali and the Twelve Imams, hold their own cem assemblies and practise a tolerant, inward faith that sets them apart from their Sunni neighbours and the Sunni Muftiate. They want the right to worship, to keep their shrines open and to protect their names and language. Their leverage lies in close-knit villages and a long habit of surviving quietly under every regime.

9.name: Ansar al-Imam
9.text:
The Partisans of the Imam are a few Yemeni students in Sofia, sons of sayyid families from the northern highlands, who were sent abroad by the republican government in Sana'a but remain loyal to the Zaydi imamate overthrown in 1962. The deposed Imam Muhammad al-Badr still claims the throne, while the long civil war between royalists and republicans moves toward a negotiated end.

They hold that rule belongs to a learned descendant of the Prophet who rises to defend the faith, as Zaydi doctrine has taught for a thousand years, and they regard the republic, Nasser's Egyptians and the communist powers as enemies of religion. Isolated and cautious, they pray together. Their leverage in Bulgaria is nil, but their families carry weight among the northern tribes.

10.name: Glavno myuftiystvo
10.text:
The Chief Mufti's Office in Sofia is the state-recognised leadership of Bulgaria's Muslims: some 800,000 Turks and well over 100,000 Pomaks and Muslim Roma. Through regional muftis in Shumen, Razgrad, Kardzhali, Plovdiv and other towns it supervises the remaining mosques and imams, under the close control of the state's committee for religious affairs and of State Security.

Loyal to the regime, the Chief Mufti endorses Bulgarian foreign policy and condemns 'reactionary' Islam, while asking for permission to train imams, repair mosques and send pilgrims to Mecca; the Banya Bashi Mosque in Sofia serves as its showcase. Its leverage is limited but real: it is the only legal voice of the Muslims, and Sofia needs it in its dealings with Turkey and the Arab world.

11.name: Usrat al-Khilafa
11.text:
The Caliphate Circle is a cell of Palestinian students at the Medical Academy and the universities of Sofia, sons of refugee families from the camps of Jordan and Lebanon, who have joined Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953. While most of their compatriots in Bulgaria study on scholarships linked to the left-wing Palestinian factions, they meet secretly to read Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani's books on the Islamic state.

They hold that the fedayeen war, Arab nationalism and Soviet friendship will never free Palestine, and that only a restored caliphate under the sharia, created by winning over army officers, can unite the Muslim world. They have no ties to Bulgaria's own Muslims. Their leverage is nil, but they carry the pan-Islamist idea into the Palestinian intelligentsia.

12.name: Deliorman ve Rodop Hocaları
12.english: Hodjas of the Deliorman and the Rhodopes
12.text:
The Hodjas of the Deliorman and the Rhodopes are the village imams, teachers and elders who hold together Bulgaria's Turkish and Pomak communities beyond the reach of the official Muftiate. They teach the Koran in private and guard Muslim names and customs under mounting pressure: Turkish schools have been merged into Bulgarian ones, and the attempt to rename the Pomaks of the Blagoevgrad district in 1964 met open resistance.

Like the Muslim Brotherhood, they seek religious revival through education, mutual aid and community discipline rather than revolt, and they defend the right to emigrate to Turkey under the agreement of 1968. Their leverage lies in the cohesion of hundreds of villages and in Ankara's attention to their fate.

13.name: Darzhavna planova komisiya
13.text:
The State Planning Committee is the headquarters of Bulgaria's command economy, drafting the five-year plans that have turned an agrarian country into an industrial one within two decades. Working with the ministries and the Council of Ministers chaired by Zhivkov himself, its planners, engineers and statisticians allocate investment to the steel works at Kremikovtsi, the chemical plants of Devnya, machine building and an electronics industry specialised within Comecon.

As a faction the planners stand for technocratic order: scientific management, computers, giant combines and specialisation within the socialist division of labour, judged by output rather than ideology. They distrust market experiments and political campaigns alike. Their leverage lies in their control of investment, supplies and statistics, and in the fact that no ministry or district can grow without their approval.

14.name: Balgarska pravoslavna tsarkva
14.text:
The Bulgarian Orthodox Church, whose patriarchate was restored in 1953, is led by Patriarch Kiril, a learned historian of the Bulgarian national revival. It lost its schools, property and youth work after 1944, saw Exarch Stefan forced out in 1948 and many priests imprisoned, and now survives under the supervision of the state's committee for religious affairs.

The Church stands for the Orthodox faith and the national tradition it carried through five centuries of Ottoman rule and the struggle for an independent exarchate. Avoiding confrontation, it supports the regime's peace campaigns abroad and asks only to keep its monasteries, from Rila to Bachkovo, alive. Its leverage lies in its place in national memory, the loyalty of older villagers and its value to the regime's patriotic cult.

15.name: Kinteks
15.text:
Kintex is the state foreign-trade company founded in Sofia in 1966 and run in practice as an arm of State Security. Behind a respectable catalogue of exports it sells weapons and ammunition to friendly regimes and liberation movements, and its officers manage transit trade through the ports of Varna and Burgas and along the roads between Western Europe and the Middle East, where the line between commerce and smuggling is thin.

As a power bloc it gathers the managers of Bulgaria's hard-currency economy: foreign trade officials, security officers and arms factory directors. They want dollar profits, freedom from the bureaucratic plan and contacts with Western, Turkish and Arab businessmen, while keeping their privileges secret. Their leverage lies in money, foreign accounts and the discreet services they render to the leadership.

16.name: Novata sistema
16.text:
The New System is the circle of economists and enterprise managers who drafted and tested the 'New System of Management of the National Economy', approved by the party in 1965 and introduced in stages from 1966. It promised enterprises a share of their profits, freedom in setting output and wages, and market signals within the plan. After the Prague Spring the leadership quietly retreated toward central control, and the reformers now wait in institutes and ministries.

They believe that Bulgaria needs profit incentives, competition, price reform and Western technology to move beyond heavy industry built on Soviet raw materials. Cautious by necessity, they present every proposal as an improvement of socialism. Their leverage lies in their expertise, the visible inefficiency of the plan and Zhivkov's own appetite for modernising experiments.

17.name: Balgarski turisticheski sayuz
17.text:
The Bulgarian Tourist Union was founded in 1895 at the call of the writer Aleko Konstantinov, who led the first mass ascent of Mount Vitosha. It is the country's great hiking and mountaineering movement, with hundreds of thousands of members, mountain huts across the Rila, Pirin, Balkan and Rhodope ranges and clubs in every town and school.

Within it gather the naturalists, foresters and mountaineers who defend the Vitosha and Pirin parks, the Rila lakes and the Black Sea dunes against quarrying, logging and the hotel building of the coast. They speak of patriotism and health rather than politics, yet their concern for clean rivers and air is the seed of an ecological conscience. Their leverage lies in their numbers, their popularity and the official cult of Bulgarian nature.

18.name: Balgarski zemedelski naroden sayuz
18.text:
The Bulgarian Agrarian National Union, founded in 1899 and led to power by Aleksandar Stamboliyski after the First World War, is the communists' only partner in the Fatherland Front. Purged of Nikola Petkov's independent wing in 1947, it keeps a mass membership, a block of seats in the National Assembly and several ministerial posts. Its leader Georgi Traykov is also Chairman of the Presidium of the National Assembly and thus head of state.

The Union accepts the leading role of the Communist Party and the cooperative farms while preserving the symbols of Stamboliyski's peasant democracy: the orange colour, rural culture and pride in the village. It speaks for the countryside within the system. Its leverage lies in its legal status and its rural network.

19.name: Gorunyovtsite
19.text:
Gorunya's Men are the heirs of the conspiracy of April 1965, when the Central Committee members Ivan Todorov-Gorunya and Tsolo Krastev and a group of officers, among them the Sofia garrison commander General Tsvyatko Anev, planned to depose Zhivkov at a party plenum with the help of the capital's tank brigade. Betrayed and arrested, Gorunya took his own life, and nine conspirators received sentences of eight to fifteen years.

Inspired by Mao Zedong, they denounced the leadership as opportunists following Khrushchev's 'revisionism' and demanded a purer, more militant Marxism-Leninism and a Bulgaria less dependent on Moscow. Their sympathisers survive among embittered partisan veterans and officers. Their leverage lies in the army's memory of the plot and in Beijing's interest in any crack in the Soviet camp.

20.name: Vazroditelite
20.text:
The Revivalists are the nationalist ideologues and district party bosses who believe that Bulgaria's Muslims must be 'returned' to the Bulgarian nation. Their first campaign, the forced renaming of Pomaks in the Blagoevgrad district in 1964, faltered amid unrest, but party committees in Smolyan and other Rhodope districts are pressing for a new and more thorough drive against Muslim names, dress and customs.

They hold that the Pomaks are Bulgarians forcibly converted under the Ottomans, that the Turks threaten national unity and that the Macedonians are Bulgarians too, and that socialism must mean one nation, one language and one culture. They exploit popular resentment of the Ottoman past and of NATO's Turkey. Their leverage lies in the party apparatus, the security services and a leadership increasingly tempted by nationalism.

21.name: Vatreshna makedonska revolyutsionna organizatsiya
21.text:
The Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization, founded in Salonica in 1893 to free Macedonia from Ottoman rule, became between the wars a state within the Bulgarian state, waging terror against Yugoslavia and its own rivals until it was banned in 1934. Its last leader, Ivan Mihailov, has lived in exile in Rome since the Second World War and guides the Macedonian Patriotic Organization of the United States and Canada through his writings.

It holds that the Macedonian Slavs are Bulgarians and seeks a Macedonia freed from Tito's Yugoslavia, independent or united with Bulgaria. Militantly anti-communist and anti-Serb, it was close to Mussolini's Italy and Pavelić's Ustaše. Its leverage lies in the émigré diaspora, the Macedonian refugee families of Sofia and Pirin, and the nationalist instincts of the Bulgarian party itself.

22.name: Balgarska narodna armiya
22.text:
The Bulgarian People's Army, about 150,000 strong, is among the most trusted forces of the Warsaw Pact, guarding its southern flank against NATO's Greece and Turkey. Defence Minister General Dobri Dzhurov, a wartime partisan commander and close ally of Zhivkov, has led it since 1962, with General Atanas Semerdzhiev as Chief of the General Staff; Bulgarian units joined the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968.

Its officers are trained in Soviet academies, equipped with Soviet weapons and watched by the Main Political Directorate, and the 1965 plot, in which generals conspired against the leadership, has kept the party vigilant. The army wants modern equipment and prestige. Its leverage lies in its role as guarantor of the regime and its close ties to the Soviet General Staff.

23.name: Dinastiya Saks-Koburg-Gota
23.text:
The House of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha-Koháry gave Bulgaria its modern monarchs, from Ferdinand, who proclaimed independence and took the title of Tsar in 1908, to Boris III and the child Tsar Simeon II, deposed by the rigged referendum of September 1946. Simeon, now 32, lives in Madrid as a businessman, married to Margarita Gómez-Acebo, and has never abdicated; on coming of age in 1955 he issued a manifesto to the nation.

The Tsar stands for a constitutional monarchy above party, national reconciliation, the Orthodox faith and Bulgaria's return to Europe. He keeps contacts with émigrés of every party. At home his name is spoken only in private, but the memory of Boris III remains warm. His leverage lies in legitimacy and his patient refusal to renounce the throne.
